places.name: Eagle Hotel
places.why: "Eagle Hotel" is a house of entertainment, and the claim that mints it (chicago_democrat_1834_05_14 c008) sets it as a display heading over its own advertisement — the building advertising itself. It is a sign and not a person: no forename or initial is ever printed as PART of it. A keeper's name is a different thing, and the house carries those — Steele's in February 1834, the taker of 15 April 1834, J. Shrigley from 1 September 1834 — which is why "the Eagle Hotel (Steele's)" merges into this record under T-0391 rather than standing beside it.

merged.merge_rule:
"Eagle Hotel" and "the Eagle Hotel (Steele's)" are one house, and the issue of 1834-02-04 is the witness that decides it — the condition this pair was held open for. Page 3, column 3 of that issue sets the name THREE TIMES in one compositor's column, twice without a keeper: at lines 2251-2260 the citizens of Chicago are called to meet "at the Ea[g]le Hotel, (Steele's)" (claim c003); ten lines below, at 2270-2281, the citizens of Cook county are called "to m[e]et [a]t the Eagle Hotel in Chicago" (c004); and at 2310-2320 an auction is cried "at the [Eag]le Hotel in this town" (c006). The setting WITH the parenthesis and the setting WITHOUT it stand ten lines apart in one column, and the two bare ones are qualified by the TOWN — "in Chicago", "in this town" — which is a paper distinguishing its Eagle from Eagles elsewhere and not from a second Eagle at home. A compositor holding two houses of one name apart for his own readers does not set the second and third without a word to tell them from the first.

AND THE SUCCESSION SAYS IT INDEPENDENTLY. The corpus follows one house it calls "the Eagle Hotel", with the definite article, through named keepers and no break: Steele's in February 1834; "he has taken the EAGLE HOTEL" over a copy date of 15 April 1834 (1834-04-16 c002, reprinted 1834-05-14 c008, 1834-06-18 c014, 1834-07-02 c004), which is a succession notice and not a building notice — the taker is a new keeper of a house that already stood; and "P. J. CARL[I], having relinquished the tav[e]rn known as the Ea[g]l[e] Hotel, on the [first of] [S]eptember last, to J. Shrigley" (1834-10-08 c006). "Known as" is the paper's own statement that the house is a single known one. The keeper who took it in April is read "P. B. F. CABLE" in some impressions and "P. J. [CARLI]" in others; WHICH the type carries is a separate question and this merge neither touches nor needs it.

SO THE PARENTHESIS IS A KEEPER, NOT A SIGN, and it is an idiom this paper uses: it writes "the Eagle Coffee House, Trowbridge's" (1835-06-24 c001) and the town carries "Graves' Tavern" the same way. The direction is into the sign, because "Eagle Hotel" is what the house sets over its own advertisement (1834-05-14 c008) while a keeper's name lasted seven months.

WHAT THIS MERGE DOES NOT REACH, stated so the next reader does not extend it. The EAGLE COFFEE HOUSE — "Trowbridge's", also "the Eagle House" — is a DIFFERENT house and is not joined here: it appears only from 1835-06-24, in or about Dearborn Street (1835-06-24 c006, 1835-08-05 c020), with its own keeper, while the Eagle Hotel is placed nowhere in the whole of 1834 and no notice gives it a street. Two houses of entertainment may share a bird. "Eagle Precinct, Lasalle county" (1834-07-30 c008) is not in Chicago at all. T-0391.

part_of.relation_rule: 'Chicago Democrat printing office' is the premises 'The Chicago Democrat' is printed at, and the two records are neither one business nor two unconnected ones. THE PAPER is read off its own imprint over John Calhoun's name, four printings between 1833-11-26 and 1834-12-03 placing it 'in the building on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets' (1833-11-26 c033, 1834-08-27 c009, 1834-09-17 c010, 1834-12-03 c023). THE SHOP is read off the paper's own colophon: 1834-01-07 c006 sets it in that same building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets, and 1835-05-20 c007 reads the colophon of that issue over Messrs. Jones & King's hardware store in the same street. WHY THIS IS NOT A MERGE: `firm_surnames()` reads the last word of each style as the partner surname and so compares {democrat} against {office}, and the partner-surname guard is right to refuse that — but neither style names a partner at all, so there is nothing here for the guard to be about, and loosening it for this pair would loosen it for every pair. WHY IT IS NOT A REFUSAL: none of the three kinds is true of it. They are not `two_houses` — one man, John Calhoun, stands over both records, and the paper and the shop that prints it are not two businesses of the town in any sense a walker would recognise. They are not `not_joined` — a printing joins them explicitly, because the colophon IS the paper naming the office it is printed at. They are not on `different_ground` — in 1834 both stand on the corner of South Water and Clark. Writing any of the three down would be a false judgement filed to make a group look closed, which is why T-0402 declined to file one. WHAT THE TOWN SHOWS, AND IT IS DECIDED HERE RATHER THAN LEFT TO FALL OUT: ONE ROOF. The roof already stands — `chicago_democrat_office`, 'The Chicago Democrat Office', which carries "John Calhoun's printing office" among its aka and is placed at that corner — and the shop enriches it. The paper did NOT: compile_register took `new_building` at `clark+south_water` for it, a second roof at the same corner for a business that has no ground of its own, because `match_occupant` requires ALL the partners' surnames and the paper's proprietors read ['John Calhoun', 'Calhoun, J.'] — a required set of {calhoun, j} that no occupant line can carry. The relation settles it: the whole follows its premises, the paper takes `enrich_existing` on `chicago_democrat_office`, and the register's actions move from 30 enrich_existing / 29 new_building to 31 / 28. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE: T-0403, which records that the office keeps its 1834 corner through T-0399's internal merge because `placement_rank` prefers a corner to a relative offset regardless of date — so on the scene date of 1835-07-01 the shop may stand at the wrong end of South Water Street, and the paper now stands with it. That is a question about placement RANKING, not about identity, and it is left open here on purpose: joining the pair moves neither reading, and answering it would mean changing how every house in the register chooses its live address. T-0403 stays open.

refused_merges.refused_because: 'W. G. Blanchard' and 'G. Blanshard' are one trade at one door and NO PRINTING IN THIS CORPUS SETS BOTH SPELLINGS, so the corpus cannot join them and this file will not join them on a resemblance. WHAT THE PAPER ACTUALLY SHOWS, and it is a great deal. Two land-agency cards run in the Chicago Democrat in 1834, one after the other and never in the same weeks: 'W. G. Blanchard' advertises “House and Land [Agent.] Lots purchased and Sold, or [by commission.] [1]2 Building Lots for sale, in th[e town and] School section. […] Houses to Let. Enquire at [the] Office on Lake st. opposite Dr. Temple's” (1834-06-11 c008, 1834-07-09 c025), and 'G. Blanshard' advertises “[HO]USES for [s]ale or to let. Also, a lot on the [cor]ner of Randolph and Wells streets, and [lots on the school section, which] will be sold [for cash. For particulars en]quire of [G. BLANSHARD], opposite Dr. Temple's, Lake-st.” (1834-10-08 c004, 1834-11-12 c012). The same landmark, the same street, the same business of selling town and school-section lots, and a gap between the two runs rather than an overlap. On the face of it that is one agent who changed his copy in the autumn, and this refusal says so rather than pretending the question is open. WHY IT IS STILL A REFUSAL. Both spellings are READ off the type and neither is a supply: 'BLANCHARD' is set in two columns the transcription does NOT flag as Tesseract fallbacks (1834-07-16 line 5527, 1834-09-17 line 3292) and 'BLANSHARD' is set whole in four impressions of its own card and again in the stray-horse reward notice of 1 October 1834 that runs beside it. So there is no misreading to repair, the way T-0408 repaired 'Branchaud' out of two fallback columns; there are two spellings the paper holds to, five weeks apart, and a forename initial that reads W in one card and F in the other. A shared anchor is two printings agreeing about a door, not one printing joining two styles — the distinction this section's `not_joined` kind exists to record, and the one C11 states for the town cards when it says a trade two men can share and a street two men can live on cannot carry an identification. The residents layer has already ruled the same way on the same initial: T-0993 holds `blanchard_w_g` distinct from `blanchard_f_gantry` under D1, noting that the Illinois land tract register carries no W. G. Blanchard at all. AND THE MACHINERY COULD NOT CARRY THE MERGE IN ANY CASE: `firm_surnames()` reads {blanchard} against {blanshard} and the partner guard refuses that with or without a rule, which is T-0407's question and not this one's. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: one printing that sets both spellings — the Democrat is caught doing exactly that for Blanshard, setting 'G. BLANSHARD' on 1834-10-01 and 'F. G. BLANSHARD' on 1834-10-22 in one standing notice — or a directory, poll or land-register entry that puts a W. G. Blanchard at the Lake Street office opposite Dr. Temple's.

anchor_change.rule: Giles Spring's office card is reset once. From 1833-12-17 to 1834-11-26 every printing sets the office 'second door west from the corner of Franklin and South Water streets', on the copy date 17 December 1833. From 1835-05-20 the card is a different one — copy-dated 3 December 1834, seven days after the last printing of the old address — and it reads 'OFFICE, first door north from the Tremont House, on Dearborn-street'. These are two crossings of this town and not two spellings of one: Franklin and South Water is on the river's south bank at the west end of the business row, and the first Tremont House stands at the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn, some four blocks east of it. The identity merge of 'Giles Spring' into 'G. Spring' already reads both cards off the page and says the second one moves him; this rule is that reading applied to the placement, not a new judgement. The corpus carries no printing of either card between 1834-11-26 and 1835-05-20, so the change is bracketed by those two dates and no closer — with the copy date of 3 December 1834 saying only when the new card was WRITTEN, which is not the same as when the office moved.
anchor_change.cannot_say: WHEN THE OFFICE ACTUALLY MOVED, AND WHETHER IT MOVED AT ALL. A card copy-dated 3 December 1834 that first appears in this deposit on 20 May 1835 leaves five and a half months in which nothing printed here says where Spring sat; the deposit is not the paper's whole run, so the new address may have been printed weeks or months before the issue that carries it, and the old one may have gone on running beside it in issues this project does not hold. Nor does anything printed say that ONE office moved rather than that a lawyer who had rooms on South Water Street took rooms on Dearborn Street: both would read exactly like this. What the rule decides is only which anchor the card is printed under at the scene date of 1835-07-01 — the Tremont House, first printed 20 May 1835 and printed again 5 August 1835 — and that is a statement about the ADVERTISEMENT. The earlier anchor is kept with its own dates and its own eleven printings so a later pass can still tell a removal from a second office. The Dearborn address is itself a count of doors, 'first door north from the Tremont House': it fixes a side of Dearborn Street and an order along it, not a lot width, and no lot is claimed for it here.

parts.relation_rule: 'Chicago Democrat printing office' is the premises 'The Chicago Democrat' is printed at, and the two records are neither one business nor two unconnected ones. THE PAPER is read off its own imprint over John Calhoun's name, four printings between 1833-11-26 and 1834-12-03 placing it 'in the building on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets' (1833-11-26 c033, 1834-08-27 c009, 1834-09-17 c010, 1834-12-03 c023). THE SHOP is read off the paper's own colophon: 1834-01-07 c006 sets it in that same building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets, and 1835-05-20 c007 reads the colophon of that issue over Messrs. Jones & King's hardware store in the same street. WHY THIS IS NOT A MERGE: `firm_surnames()` reads the last word of each style as the partner surname and so compares {democrat} against {office}, and the partner-surname guard is right to refuse that — but neither style names a partner at all, so there is nothing here for the guard to be about, and loosening it for this pair would loosen it for every pair. WHY IT IS NOT A REFUSAL: none of the three kinds is true of it. They are not `two_houses` — one man, John Calhoun, stands over both records, and the paper and the shop that prints it are not two businesses of the town in any sense a walker would recognise. They are not `not_joined` — a printing joins them explicitly, because the colophon IS the paper naming the office it is printed at. They are not on `different_ground` — in 1834 both stand on the corner of South Water and Clark. Writing any of the three down would be a false judgement filed to make a group look closed, which is why T-0402 declined to file one. WHAT THE TOWN SHOWS, AND IT IS DECIDED HERE RATHER THAN LEFT TO FALL OUT: ONE ROOF. The roof already stands — `chicago_democrat_office`, 'The Chicago Democrat Office', which carries "John Calhoun's printing office" among its aka and is placed at that corner — and the shop enriches it. The paper did NOT: compile_register took `new_building` at `clark+south_water` for it, a second roof at the same corner for a business that has no ground of its own, because `match_occupant` requires ALL the partners' surnames and the paper's proprietors read ['John Calhoun', 'Calhoun, J.'] — a required set of {calhoun, j} that no occupant line can carry. The relation settles it: the whole follows its premises, the paper takes `enrich_existing` on `chicago_democrat_office`, and the register's actions move from 30 enrich_existing / 29 new_building to 31 / 28. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE: T-0403, which records that the office keeps its 1834 corner through T-0399's internal merge because `placement_rank` prefers a corner to a relative offset regardless of date — so on the scene date of 1835-07-01 the shop may stand at the wrong end of South Water Street, and the paper now stands with it. That is a question about placement RANKING, not about identity, and it is left open here on purpose: joining the pair moves neither reading, and answering it would mean changing how every house in the register chooses its live address. T-0403 stays open.

refused_merges.refused_because: 'W. G. Blanchard' and 'G. Blanshard' are one trade at one door and NO PRINTING IN THIS CORPUS SETS BOTH SPELLINGS, so the corpus cannot join them and this file will not join them on a resemblance. WHAT THE PAPER ACTUALLY SHOWS, and it is a great deal. Two land-agency cards run in the Chicago Democrat in 1834, one after the other and never in the same weeks: 'W. G. Blanchard' advertises “House and Land [Agent.] Lots purchased and Sold, or [by commission.] [1]2 Building Lots for sale, in th[e town and] School section. […] Houses to Let. Enquire at [the] Office on Lake st. opposite Dr. Temple's” (1834-06-11 c008, 1834-07-09 c025), and 'G. Blanshard' advertises “[HO]USES for [s]ale or to let. Also, a lot on the [cor]ner of Randolph and Wells streets, and [lots on the school section, which] will be sold [for cash. For particulars en]quire of [G. BLANSHARD], opposite Dr. Temple's, Lake-st.” (1834-10-08 c004, 1834-11-12 c012). The same landmark, the same street, the same business of selling town and school-section lots, and a gap between the two runs rather than an overlap. On the face of it that is one agent who changed his copy in the autumn, and this refusal says so rather than pretending the question is open. WHY IT IS STILL A REFUSAL. Both spellings are READ off the type and neither is a supply: 'BLANCHARD' is set in two columns the transcription does NOT flag as Tesseract fallbacks (1834-07-16 line 5527, 1834-09-17 line 3292) and 'BLANSHARD' is set whole in four impressions of its own card and again in the stray-horse reward notice of 1 October 1834 that runs beside it. So there is no misreading to repair, the way T-0408 repaired 'Branchaud' out of two fallback columns; there are two spellings the paper holds to, five weeks apart, and a forename initial that reads W in one card and F in the other. A shared anchor is two printings agreeing about a door, not one printing joining two styles — the distinction this section's `not_joined` kind exists to record, and the one C11 states for the town cards when it says a trade two men can share and a street two men can live on cannot carry an identification. The residents layer has already ruled the same way on the same initial: T-0993 holds `blanchard_w_g` distinct from `blanchard_f_gantry` under D1, noting that the Illinois land tract register carries no W. G. Blanchard at all. AND THE MACHINERY COULD NOT CARRY THE MERGE IN ANY CASE: `firm_surnames()` reads {blanchard} against {blanshard} and the partner guard refuses that with or without a rule, which is T-0407's question and not this one's. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: one printing that sets both spellings — the Democrat is caught doing exactly that for Blanshard, setting 'G. BLANSHARD' on 1834-10-01 and 'F. G. BLANSHARD' on 1834-10-22 in one standing notice — or a directory, poll or land-register entry that puts a W. G. Blanchard at the Lake Street office opposite Dr. Temple's.

agencies.why: The Howard Fire Insurance Company is a New York company that never stood in this town. It sold fire insurance in Chicago through a LOCAL AGENT, and one standing advertisement — the same setting word for word, only the signature and the number of the verb changing — runs across thirteen months of the corpus: 'THE subscribers having been appointed Agents for the Howard Fire Insurance Company of the city of New-York, for Chicago and the vicinity, will insure property against loss by Fire, on reasonable terms. HUBBARD & CO.' from 1834-07-02, and the identical copy in the SINGULAR over one man, 'THE subscriber having been appointed Agent … E. K. HUBBARD.', from 1835-06-20. Neither the company nor the agency is a house in this town: no printing gives either a street, and nothing here decides whether E. K. Hubbard was a partner in Hubbard & Co., because no printing says so.

holdings.note: Hubbard & Co. held the agency first and advertised it in the PLURAL over the firm's own signature: '[The su]bscribers having been appointed [Ag]ents for the Howard Fire Insurance [Company of] the city of New-York … HUBBARD & CO.' (1834-07-02 c048). The 1834-10-15 c005 and 1835-05-20 c023 printings are the same setting over the copy date 'July 1'. The plural verb and the firm signature are the whole of what makes this the FIRM's holding rather than a partner's, and it is all they make it: the commission and forwarding house gains a line on its card and nothing else — no trade, no street, no roof. 'fire insurance' stands in this record's goods because the notice ran over its signature, which is a fact about the printing and not a second trade.

From 1835-06-20 the identical copy runs in the SINGULAR over one man — 'THE su[bs]criber ha[v]ing been [a]p[poin]t[e]d [agent] for the Howard Fire Insurance [Company] … E. K. [H]UBBARD.', American 1835-06-20 c015, copy-dated June 20, 1835 — and the Democrat reprints it at 1835-07-01 c017, 1835-07-08 c005, 1835-07-29 c011 and 1835-08-05 c008 over the copy date 'July 1'. So on the scene date the agency sits with E. K. Hubbard, and the forwarding house goes on trading under its own name to 1835-08-29. This project never reads a shared surname with different initials as one man, so the holder here is the MAN the signature names and nothing joins him to Hubbard & Co.'s partners, Gurdon S. Hubbard and Henry G. Hubbard. That refusal is exactly what the old `refused_firm_merges` entry was for, and it is what this relation replaces: the two records are not confused, they are joined — by an agency that passed from the firm to one man.

refused_holdings.refused_because: T-0410 was filed reading a THIRD holder off 1835-08-05 c008, where the agency notice is claimed on the Jones, King & Co. business record and that record therefore announced itself 'appointed Agent for the Howard Fire Insurance Company'. The fragment refutes it. Its own reading runs 'July 1, [1835]. [E]. K. [H]UBBARD. — Hardware, Stoves, &c. Th[e] u[n]dersigned have [formed a] connect[ion] in the mercantile business, under the [f]irm o[f] Jones, [King] & [C]o.': two notices on one fragment, as that claim's own notes say, and the fire-insurance card is signed by the man while the hardware notice below it is signed WILLIAM JONES, BYRAM KING, W. B. CLARKE. The claim's own entity list reads 'UCBRARB,' as 'Hubbard, E. K.' with the role 'insurance agent'. Nothing in the setting puts the agency in Jones, King & Co.'s hands; the segmenter put the two advertisements on one line. So there is no handover in the week of 5 August, and this is the fifth printing of the E. K. Hubbard holding above. The claim's `announces_opening` is dropped in the same pass, because it was the agency's sentence read onto the hardware firm's record.
